unit.title: Life cycles of flowering plants
unit.blurb: Flowers, bees, fruits, flying seeds and germination – the whole life cycle of a flowering plant.

O1.t: Sort plants into flowering and non-flowering plants, and name the parts of a flower and their jobs.

O2.t: Describe pollination by insects and wind, fertilisation, and how the ovary becomes a fruit with seeds.

O3.t: Explain why seeds are dispersed and describe dispersal by wind, animals, water and exploding pods.

O4.t: Plan a fair test with model seeds, repeat measurements and find an average.

O5.t: Describe the conditions seeds need to germinate and the life cycle of a flowering plant.

captions: Hello, plant detectives! Grab your magnifying glass.
This is lesson 1.1: flowering and non-flowering plants.
Let's go on a plant hunt in the park. Look, an apple tree covered in flowers!
And here is a sunflower, with one giant flower, as big as your face.
But wait. This fern has no flowers at all. Not even one. How strange!
Scientists sort plants into two big groups.
Flowering plants grow flowers, and their flowers make seeds.
Non-flowering plants never grow flowers. Ferns and mosses make tiny spores instead, and pine trees make cones.
Pause and think. Is a fern a flowering plant, or a non-flowering plant?
Turn a fern leaf over. Can you see little brown dots? They are full of spores.
Spores are as light as dust, so the wind carries them far away.
If a spore lands somewhere damp and shady, a brand new fern grows. Clever!
Did you know? The biggest flower in the world can be as wide as a car tyre.
And it smells like rotten meat! Pee-yew! The smell attracts flies, which carry its pollen.
Let's zoom in on a flower. Every part has a job.
The bright petals attract insects, like a big sign saying: come here!
The stamens are the male parts. They make yellow pollen.
The carpel is the female part. Seeds grow inside it. And the green sepals protected the flower when it was a bud.
Joke time! What did the big flower say to the little flower?
Hi, bud! A bud is a flower that has not opened yet.
Your turn. Which part of a flower makes pollen?
Let's be flower scientists.
Ask an adult for a large flower, like a lily, and gently pull off the parts.
Sort them into groups: petals, sepals, stamens and the carpel.
Then stick them on paper and label them. Wash your hands afterwards!
Let's remember.
Flowering plants grow flowers, and the flowers make seeds.
Non-flowering plants, like ferns and mosses, make spores instead.
Petals attract insects, and stamens make pollen.
And seeds grow inside the carpel.
Brilliant detective work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Buzz buzz! Hello again, plant detectives!
This is lesson 1.2: pollination, fruits and seeds.
Meet Bella the bee. She lands on a flower to drink sweet nectar.
Oops! Yellow pollen sticks all over her furry body.
Then Bella flies to the next flower of the same kind.
Some of the pollen rubs off onto the top of the carpel, called the stigma. Bella has just done a very important job!
Moving pollen from a stamen to a stigma is called pollination.
Insects like bees and butterflies carry pollen from flower to flower.
Some plants, like grasses, let the wind carry their pollen instead.
Wind flowers are usually small and plain. They do not need to show off for insects!
Pause and think. What is pollination?
After pollination, the pollen joins with an egg cell inside the carpel. This is called fertilisation.
Now the flower does not need its petals any more, so they fall off.
The bottom of the carpel, the ovary, swells up and becomes a fruit.
And inside the fruit are the seeds. Every apple core is a seed treasure box!
Here is a surprise. To a scientist, a tomato is a fruit, because it has seeds inside.
A cucumber is a fruit too. Look at the seeds in the middle.
And so is a pepper. If it grew from a flower and holds seeds, it is a fruit!
Did you know? A strawberry is the only common fruit that wears its seeds on the outside.
One strawberry has about two hundred seeds. Try counting them!
Your turn. Which part of the flower becomes the fruit?
Let's investigate seeds.
Ask an adult to cut an apple, an orange, a tomato and a pepper in half.
Count the seeds in each fruit and record the numbers in a table.
Which fruit has the most seeds? Make a prediction first!
Let's remember.
Pollination is when pollen moves from a stamen to a stigma.
Insects or the wind carry the pollen.
Fertilisation is when pollen joins with an egg cell.
And the ovary becomes a fruit, with seeds inside.
Buzzing good work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, seed explorers! Get ready for a seed adventure.
This is lesson 1.3: how seeds are spread.
Imagine all of a tree's seeds fell right underneath it. Squash!
The little plants would fight with each other, and with their parent, for light, water and space.
So plants send their seeds away. Spreading seeds is called seed dispersal.
Pause and think. Why do plants need to spread their seeds?
Some seeds fly! Blow on a dandelion clock, and each seed floats away on a tiny parachute.
Sycamore seeds have wings. They spin like little helicopters as they fall.
This is wind dispersal. Wind seeds are light, with wings or hairs.
Animals help too. A bird gobbles a juicy berry.
It flies far away, with the seed inside its tummy.
Later, the seed comes out in the bird's poo, with free fertiliser. Yuck, but very useful!
Other seeds, called burrs, have tiny hooks that catch on animal fur, or on your socks. This is animal dispersal.
A coconut can float across the sea for weeks, and grow on a faraway beach.
Some pods dry out in the sun, and twist and twist…
Until, pop! They explode and shoot their seeds out. Ready, steady, go!
Riddle time! I have no wings, but I can fly. I have a parachute, but I am not a soldier. What am I?
A dandelion seed!
Your turn. How are burrs spread?
Let's make model sycamore seeds.
Make paper helicopters with short, medium and long wings.
Drop each one from the same height, and time how long it takes to land.
Repeat each test three times. Do longer wings make a seed fall more slowly?
Let's remember.
Seed dispersal moves seeds away from the parent plant.
Wind seeds have parachutes or wings.
Animals eat berries, or carry burrs on their fur.
Some seeds float on water, and some pods explode.
Fantastic exploring! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Hello, super growers! Let's wake up some seeds.
This is lesson 1.4: seed germination.
A seed is like a tiny lunch box. Inside is a baby plant and a store of food.
When the conditions are right, the seed starts to grow. First a root pushes down, then a shoot pushes up. This is called germination.
To germinate, a seed needs water, warmth and air.
Pause and think. What three things does a seed need to germinate?
Here is a surprise. Put a damp seed in a dark cupboard.
It still germinates! Seeds use their food store, so they do not need light to start.
But once the leaves open, the young plant needs light to make its own food.
Try planting a bean upside down. Will it get confused?
No! The root always turns and grows down, towards water.
And the shoot always turns and grows up, towards the light. Plants are clever!
Did you know? Scientists found some date palm seeds that were about two thousand years old.
They planted one, and it germinated! Some seeds can wait a very, very long time.
Now we can join everything into a circle, called a life cycle.
Seed, germination, young plant, flowering, pollination, then fruit and seeds.
And the new seeds start the circle all over again. Round and round it goes!
Your turn. In the life cycle, what comes after pollination?
Let's plan a fair test.
Put cress seeds on cotton wool in two dishes.
Water one dish, and keep the other dish dry. Keep everything else the same, like warmth.
Check every day for a week, and count how many seeds germinate in each dish.
Let's remember.
Germination is when a seed starts to grow.
A seed needs water, warmth and air to germinate.
The root grows down, and the shoot grows up.
And the life cycle goes from seed, to plant, to flower, to fruit, and back to seed.
Super growing! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.
